source_refs.note: Chapter 6 exercise (PDF 140-143), solved: 12 MCQs keyed from the chapter (no key is printed), 12 short and 2 descriptive questions with model answers, 6 numericals worked step by step. MCQ I-II, Q.5, Q.6, Q.8 and Q.10 carry Book corrections.

blocks.text: Q.1 Four choices are given for each question. Select the correct choice.

blocks.prompt: I. Which of the following equations represents standard heat of formation of C₂H₄?
blocks.explanation: Standard enthalpy of formation: one mole of the compound formed from its elements in their standard states (6.3.3). The standard state of carbon is graphite, not diamond, and of hydrogen is H₂(g), not H atoms; (c) forms only ½ mol C₂H₄.

blocks.prompt: II. Which of the following equations correctly defines lattice energy of MgCl₂?
blocks.explanation: Lattice energy is the enthalpy change when one mole of the ionic compound (solid) is formed from its gaseous ions (6.9.2). Only (d) starts from gaseous ions and ends with the solid. (a) is the enthalpy of formation.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In MCQs I and II the arrow between reactants and products is not printed (a blank gap is left); → is written here.

blocks.prompt: III. Suppose there are 100 molecules of a gas initially in jar A, which is connected to an evacuated jar B. When the stopcock is opened the possible ways of arrangement of molecules will be:
blocks.explanation: Number of possible arrangements = xʸ, where x = number of places (2 jars) and y = number of particles (100): 2¹⁰⁰ (6.11.1).

blocks.prompt: IV. For a reaction to occur spontaneously,
blocks.explanation: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, and a process is spontaneous when ΔG < 0 (6.12). A negative ΔH or ΔS alone does not decide spontaneity.

blocks.prompt: V. The calorie content of food, often expressed in Calories (kcal), is fundamentally related to which thermodynamic quantity during its metabolism or combustion?
blocks.explanation: The calorie content of a food is its enthalpy of combustion (ΔHc) expressed in kilocalories per gram (6.7.1); digestion releases the same energy as burning.

blocks.prompt: VI. Which of the following quantities is NOT typically determined using Hess’s Law?
blocks.explanation: Hess's law deals with enthalpy changes between initial and final states, independent of route. Activation energy depends on the path (the energy barrier) and comes from rate studies, not from Hess cycles.

blocks.prompt: VII. Which of the following factors would lead to a greater enthalpy change of hydration (more exothermic)?

options.text: A larger ionic radius and a smaller charge
A smaller ionic radius and a smaller charge
A larger ionic radius and a larger charge
A smaller ionic radius and a larger charge

blocks.explanation: Greater charge on a smaller ion means a higher charge density, so water molecules are attracted more strongly and more energy is released (6.9.1), e.g. Na⁺ < Mg²⁺ < Al³⁺.

blocks.prompt: VIII. The enthalpy of solution can be expressed in terms of which of the following enthalpy changes?
blocks.explanation: From the energy cycle (6.9.3): ΔH°latt + ΔH°sol = ΔH°hyd, so ΔH°sol = −ΔH°latt + ΔH°hyd. Here lattice energy is defined for forming the solid from gaseous ions, so dissolving the solid uses −ΔH°latt.

blocks.prompt: IX. Which of the following reactions has an enthalpy change that is equal to the standard enthalpy of formation of water, ΔH°f[H₂O(l)]?
blocks.explanation: One mole of liquid water formed from its elements in their standard states, H₂(g) and O₂(g). (a) uses atoms, (b) gives steam, (d) uses ions.

blocks.prompt: X. The enthalpy change for a reaction depends on:

options.text: Pathway taken from reactants to products
Initial and final states of the reactants and products

blocks.explanation: By Hess's law the total enthalpy change is independent of the route; it depends only on the initial and final states (6.8).

blocks.prompt: XI. Which of the following processes would typically result in an increase in entropy of the system?

options.text: Dissolving a solid in a liquid
Formation of a crystal from a saturated solution

blocks.explanation: Dissolving spreads the solute particles through the liquid, increasing the number of ways of arrangement, e.g. sugar dissolving in tea increases entropy (6.11.2). The other three make the system more ordered.

blocks.prompt: XII. Consider a reaction with ΔH>0 and ΔS<0. This reaction will be:
blocks.explanation: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. With ΔH positive and −TΔS also positive (ΔS negative), ΔG is positive at every temperature, so the reaction is never spontaneous.

blocks.text: Q.2 Attempt the following short-answer questions:

blocks.prompt: a. Differentiate between exothermic and endothermic reactions.
blocks.explanation: They differ in the direction of heat flow and the sign of ΔH.

rows: Heat is evolved from the system to the surroundings
Heat is absorbed by the system from the surroundings
H(products) < H(reactants)
H(products) > H(reactants)
ΔH is negative
ΔH is positive
Surroundings get warmer
Surroundings get cooler
C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −393.7 kJ mol⁻¹
NH₄Cl(s) dissolving in water, ΔH = +16.2 kJ mol⁻¹

blocks.prompt: b. What do you understand by the enthalpy of a system?
blocks.explanation: Enthalpy (heat content), H, is the energy possessed by a substance due to its structure (types of bonds) and physical state. Its absolute value cannot be measured; only the change ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants), the heat evolved or absorbed at constant pressure, is measured (6.1).

blocks.prompt: c. Differentiate clearly between entropy (S) and Gibbs free energy (G).
blocks.explanation: They are linked by G = H − TS (ΔG = ΔH − TΔS).

rows: Measure of the number of ways energy can be distributed; randomness or disorder
Part of the enthalpy that is free to be converted into useful work
Unit: J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
Unit: kJ mol⁻¹
ΔS = S(products) − S(reactants)
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS
ΔS alone cannot always predict spontaneity
ΔG < 0 spontaneous; ΔG > 0 non-spontaneous; ΔG = 0 equilibrium
S of a substance is always positive
ΔG can be positive, negative or zero

blocks.prompt: d. Distinguish clearly between standard enthalpy of reaction and standard enthalpy of formation.
blocks.explanation: Enthalpy of formation is a special case of enthalpy of reaction.

rows: Enthalpy change when stoichiometric amounts of reactants react completely under standard conditions
Enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements under standard conditions
Any reaction; reactants may be compounds
Reactants are only elements in their standard states
Amount as in the balanced equation
Always for one mole of product
e.g. C₂H₄ + HCl → C₂H₅Cl, ΔH = −68.9 kJ mol⁻¹
e.g. C(s) + 2H₂(g) → CH₄(g), ΔH°f = −74.8 kJ mol⁻¹

blocks.prompt:
e. Define the following enthalpies and give one example of each.
(i) Standard enthalpy of solution (ii) Standard enthalpy of hydration
(iii) Standard enthalpy of atomization (iv) Standard enthalpy of combustion
blocks.explanation:
(i) Standard enthalpy of solution: heat absorbed or evolved when one mole of a substance dissolves in a solvent to give an infinitely dilute solution. NH₄Cl(s) + aq → NH₄⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq), ΔH°sol = +16.2 kJ mol⁻¹.
(ii) Standard enthalpy of hydration: enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous ions dissolves in excess water to give an infinitely dilute solution; always exothermic. Na⁺(g) + aq → Na⁺(aq), ΔH°hyd = −406 kJ mol⁻¹.
(iii) Standard enthalpy of atomization: enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms is formed from the element under standard conditions. ½H₂(g) → H(g), ΔH°at = +218 kJ mol⁻¹.
(iv) Standard enthalpy of combustion: enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is completely burnt in excess oxygen under standard conditions; always exothermic. C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l), ΔH°c = −1368 kJ mol⁻¹.

blocks.prompt: f. Explain why the lattice enthalpy of an ionic compound is typically a large negative value.
blocks.explanation: Lattice enthalpy is for forming one mole of the solid from gaseous ions. Oppositely charged ions come together and strong electrostatic attractions (ionic bonds) form in all directions of the three-dimensional lattice; bond formation releases energy, so ΔH is negative and large, e.g. NaCl −787 kJ mol⁻¹, MgO −3923 kJ mol⁻¹.

blocks.prompt: g. What factors influence the magnitude of the lattice enthalpy?
blocks.explanation:
1. Charge on the ions: greater charge gives stronger attraction and larger lattice energy, e.g. MgO (−3923 kJ mol⁻¹) > LiF (−1049 kJ mol⁻¹), ions of similar size.
2. Size of the ions: smaller ions pack more tightly, so lattice energy is larger; it decreases as cation or anion size increases (e.g. alkali metal halides from LiF to CsI) (6.9.2).

blocks.prompt: h. Explain why the enthalpy of hydration is always an exothermic process for gaseous ions. What are the main interactions responsible for the release of energy during hydration?
blocks.explanation:
During hydration no bonds are broken; free gaseous ions only attract polar water molecules and new attractions form, so energy is always released.
Interactions: ion-dipole forces. A cation attracts the δ− oxygen ends of water molecules; an anion attracts the δ+ hydrogen ends. The ion becomes surrounded by water molecules (hydrated). Higher charge density gives stronger ion-dipole forces and more energy released (6.9.1).

blocks.prompt: i. For the reaction CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g), identify all the bonds that need to be broken and all the bonds that need to be formed to carry out a bond energy calculation of ΔH.
blocks.explanation:
Bonds broken (reactants): 4 C–H bonds in CH₄ and 2 O=O bonds in 2O₂.
Bonds formed (products): 2 C=O bonds in CO₂ and 4 O–H bonds in 2H₂O.
Then ΔH = Σ(energies of bonds broken) − Σ(energies of bonds formed) = [4E(C–H) + 2E(O=O)] − [2E(C=O) + 4E(O–H)] (6.8).

blocks.prompt: j. For a reaction to be spontaneous, what is the required sign of the Gibbs free energy change (ΔG)? Under what conditions of enthalpy change (ΔH) and entropy change (ΔS) will a reaction always be spontaneous?
blocks.explanation:
ΔG must be negative (ΔG < 0).
Since ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, a reaction is spontaneous at all temperatures when ΔH is negative (exothermic) and ΔS is positive; then both terms make ΔG negative at every temperature.

blocks.prompt: k. The enthalpy of solution can be either positive or negative. Explain what a positive ΔHsol and a negative ΔHsol indicate about the energy changes during the dissolution process.
blocks.explanation:
Dissolving needs energy to break the lattice (and separate solvent molecules) and releases energy in hydration (ΔH°sol = ΔH°hyd − ΔH°latt).
Positive ΔHsol: energy absorbed to break the lattice is more than the hydration energy released; endothermic, the solution cools (NH₄Cl, +16.2 kJ mol⁻¹).
Negative ΔHsol: hydration energy released is more than the energy needed to break the lattice; exothermic, the solution warms (Na₂CO₃, −25 kJ mol⁻¹).

blocks.prompt: l. Consider two ions with similar charges but different sizes, or similar sizes but different charges. Explain how the concept of charge density can be used to predict which ion will have a more exothermic enthalpy of hydration and why.
blocks.explanation:
Charge density = charge per unit size (area) of the ion. The ion with higher charge density attracts the polar water molecules more strongly, so more energy is released and its hydration is more exothermic.
Same charge, different size: the smaller ion wins, e.g. Mg²⁺ > Ca²⁺ > Sr²⁺.
Same size, different charge: the more highly charged ion wins, e.g. Na⁺ < Mg²⁺ < Al³⁺ (6.9.1).

blocks.prompt: Q.3 State and explain Hess’ law. Give its two applications.
blocks.explanation:
Statement: The total enthalpy change in a chemical reaction is independent of the route by which the reaction takes place, as long as the initial and final conditions are the same.
Explanation: Hess's law applies the law of conservation of energy to enthalpy changes. Suppose A is converted into B directly (ΔHr) or by indirect routes through intermediates: route 1, A → M → B (ΔH₁, ΔH₂); route 2, A → X → Y → B (ΔH₃, ΔH₄, ΔH₅). Then
ΔHr = ΔH₁ + ΔH₂ = ΔH₃ + ΔH₄ + ΔH₅
If the sums were different, energy could be created by going one way and returning the other, which is impossible.
Example: C(graphite) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹ (direct), or C(graphite) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g), ΔH₁, then CO(g) + ½O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH₂ = −283 kJ mol⁻¹. So ΔH₁ = −393.5 − (−283) = −110.5 kJ mol⁻¹.
Applications:
1. Enthalpy changes that cannot be measured directly, e.g. the enthalpy of formation of CO (above), CCl₄ or C₆H₆, from enthalpies of combustion.
2. Lattice energy of an ionic compound from the Born-Haber cycle, e.g. NaCl, −787 kJ mol⁻¹.
(Also: ΔHr from enthalpies of formation, ΔHr from bond energies, and the enthalpy of solution from lattice and hydration energies.)

blocks.prompt: Q.4 What is lattice energy? How does Born-Haber cycle help to calculate the lattice energy of NaCl?
blocks.explanation:
Lattice energy: the enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic compound is formed from its gaseous ions under standard conditions; it is always negative.
Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) → NaCl(s), ΔH°latt = ?
It cannot be measured by one direct experiment, so it is found from Hess's law using the Born-Haber cycle.
The cycle (energy triangle): formation of NaCl directly from its elements (ΔH°f), or indirectly by first changing the elements into gaseous ions (ΔHx) and then forming the solid from these ions (ΔH°latt):
ΔHx + ΔH°latt = ΔH°f
Steps of ΔHx:
1. Atomization of sodium: Na(s) → Na(g), ΔHat = +108 kJ mol⁻¹
2. Ionization of sodium: Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻, ΔHi1 = +496 kJ mol⁻¹
3. Atomization of chlorine: ½Cl₂(g) → Cl(g), ΔHat = +121 kJ mol⁻¹
4. Electron affinity of chlorine: Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g), ΔHea1 = −349 kJ mol⁻¹
ΔHx = 108 + 496 + 121 + (−349) = +376 kJ mol⁻¹
Enthalpy of formation (measured in a calorimeter): Na(s) + ½Cl₂(g) → NaCl(s), ΔH°f = −411 kJ mol⁻¹
So ΔH°latt = ΔH°f − ΔHx = −411 − 376 = −787 kJ mol⁻¹

blocks.prompt: Q.5 (a) When 0.400 g NaOH is dissolved in 100.0 g of water, the temperature rises from 25.00 to 26.03 °C. Calculate: (i). qwater, (ii). ΔH for the solution process
blocks.explanation:
Given: m(water) = 100.0 g, c(water) = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹, ΔT = 26.03 − 25.00 = 1.03 °C, mass of NaOH = 0.400 g, molar mass of NaOH = 40.0 g mol⁻¹
(i) q(water) = m × c × ΔT
q = 100.0 g × 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ × 1.03 °C
q = 431 J = 0.431 kJ (heat absorbed by the water)
(ii) Moles of NaOH: n = 0.400 g / 40.0 g mol⁻¹ = 0.0100 mol
The heat absorbed by the water was released by the dissolving NaOH, so the process is exothermic.
ΔH = −q / n = −0.431 kJ / 0.0100 mol
ΔH = −43.1 kJ mol⁻¹
Answers: q(water) = +431 J; ΔH(solution) = −43.1 kJ mol⁻¹

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Q.5 is printed with part '(a)' only; no part (b) follows.

blocks.prompt:
Q.6 By applying Hess’ law, calculate the enthalpy change for the formation of an aqueous solution of NH₄Cl from NH₃ gas and HCl gas. The results for the various reactions are as follows.
(i) NH₃(g) + aq → NH₃(aq)  ΔH = –35.16 kJ mol⁻¹
(ii) HCl(g) + aq → HCl(aq)  ΔH = –72.41 kJ mol⁻¹
(iii) NH₃(aq) + HCl(aq) → NH₄Cl(aq)  ΔH = –51.48 kJ mol⁻¹
blocks.explanation:
Required: NH₃(g) + HCl(g) + aq → NH₄Cl(aq), ΔH = ?
Adding equations (i), (ii) and (iii), NH₃(aq) and HCl(aq) cancel and the required equation is left. By Hess's law:
ΔH = ΔH(i) + ΔH(ii) + ΔH(iii)
ΔH = (−35.16) + (−72.41) + (−51.48) kJ mol⁻¹
ΔH = −159.05 kJ mol⁻¹
Answer: −159.05 kJ mol⁻¹

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the printed equations the arrow stands after the product (e.g. 'NH₃(g) + aq NH₃(aq) → ΔH = ...'); it belongs between reactants and products, as written here.

blocks.prompt:
Q.7 Calculate the heat of formation of ethyl alcohol from the following information
(i) Heat of combustion of ethyl alcohol is –1367 kJ mol⁻¹
(ii) Heat of formation of carbon dioxide is –393.7 kJ mol⁻¹
(iii) Heat of formation of water is –285.8 kJ mol⁻¹
blocks.explanation:
Required: 2C(graphite) + 3H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → C₂H₅OH(l), ΔH°f = ?
Combustion: C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l), ΔH°c = −1367 kJ mol⁻¹
Hess's law: ΔH°c = [2ΔH°f(CO₂) + 3ΔH°f(H₂O)] − [ΔH°f(C₂H₅OH) + 3ΔH°f(O₂)], with ΔH°f(O₂) = 0
So ΔH°f(C₂H₅OH) = 2ΔH°f(CO₂) + 3ΔH°f(H₂O) − ΔH°c
= 2(−393.7) + 3(−285.8) − (−1367) kJ mol⁻¹
= −787.4 − 857.4 + 1367 kJ mol⁻¹
= −277.8 kJ mol⁻¹
Answer: heat of formation of ethyl alcohol = −277.8 kJ mol⁻¹

blocks.prompt:
Q8 Using the information given in the table below, calculate the lattice energy of potassium bromide.
(Table printed, reactions with ΔH/kJ mol⁻¹: K(s) + ½Br₂(l) → K⁺Br⁻, −392; K(s) → K(g), +90; K(s) → K⁺(g) + e⁻, +420; ½Br₂(l) → Br(g), +112; Br + e⁻ → Br⁻, −342.)
blocks.explanation:
Born-Haber cycle: ΔH°f = ΔHat(K) + IE(K) + ΔHat(Br) + EA(Br) + ΔH°latt
Given: ΔH°f = −392, ΔHat(K) = +90, IE(K) = +420, ΔHat(Br) = +112, EA(Br) = −342 (all kJ mol⁻¹)
ΔHx = 90 + 420 + 112 + (−342) = +280 kJ mol⁻¹
ΔH°latt = ΔH°f − ΔHx
ΔH°latt = −392 − 280 kJ mol⁻¹
ΔH°latt = −672 kJ mol⁻¹
Answer: lattice energy of KBr = −672 kJ mol⁻¹ (K⁺(g) + Br⁻(g) → KBr(s))

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the table the ionization step is printed 'K(s) → K⁺(g) + e⁻'; ionization energy starts from the gaseous atom: K(g) → K⁺(g) + e⁻, +420 kJ mol⁻¹. The other rows lack state symbols: KBr is the solid, K⁺Br⁻(s), and the last step is Br(g) + e⁻ → Br⁻(g).

blocks.prompt:
Q.9 Calculate the entropy change of the surroundings ΔS°surrounding for the reaction at 298K :
2Ca(s) + O₂(g) → 2CaO(s)  ΔH°reaction = –1270.2 kJ mol⁻¹
blocks.explanation:
Given: ΔH°reaction = −1270.2 kJ mol⁻¹ = −1270.2 × 10³ J mol⁻¹, T = 298 K
Formula: the heat released by the system is absorbed by the surroundings, so ΔS°surroundings = −ΔH°reaction / T
Substitution: ΔS°surroundings = −(−1270.2 × 10³ J mol⁻¹) / 298 K
ΔS°surroundings = +4262 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = +4.26 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
Answer: +4.26 × 10³ J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. It is far larger than the decrease in the entropy of the system (−208.4 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, 6.11.4), so the total entropy increases and calcium burns spontaneously.

blocks.prompt:
Q.10 For the reaction: CaSO₄(s) → Ca²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq)
Calculate ΔH°, ΔS° and ΔG° at 25 °C using the following data; and discuss its spontaneity.
Enthalpy of Formation:
ΔH°f (CaSO₄(s)) = -1432.7 kJ, ΔH°f (Ca²⁺(aq)) = -543.0 kJ, ΔH°f (SO₄²⁻(aq)) = -907.5 kJ
[Standard entropy: S°(CaSO₄(s)) = 106.7 J/K, S°(Ca²⁺(aq)) = –55.2 J/K, S°(SO₄²⁻(aq)) = +17.2 J/K]
blocks.explanation:
ΔH° = ΣΔH°f(products) − ΣΔH°f(reactants)
ΔH° = [(−543.0) + (−907.5)] − (−1432.7) kJ = −1450.5 + 1432.7 kJ = −17.8 kJ
ΔS° = ΣS°(products) − ΣS°(reactants)
ΔS° = [(−55.2) + 17.2] − 106.7 J/K = −38.0 − 106.7 J/K = −144.7 J/K = −0.1447 kJ/K
ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°, T = 25 + 273 = 298 K
ΔG° = (−17.8 kJ) − (298 K × −0.1447 kJ/K)
ΔG° = −17.8 kJ + 43.1 kJ = +25.3 kJ
Result: ΔG° is positive, so the dissolution of CaSO₄ is non-spontaneous under standard conditions at 25 °C. The favourable (negative) ΔH is outweighed by the decrease in entropy (−TΔS = +43.1 kJ).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Q.10 repeats Sample Problem 6.12 of the chapter with the same data; the answer, ΔG° = +25.3 kJ, agrees with the sample's result.
